Record * Alt+X (Level Scaling) is the one that changes how you build risers and automation curves — most producers manually drag every point instead of scaling all at once ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ * These are felt more than heard — the listener won't consciously notice any single one, but they'll notice if the drop feels flat without them * Start by adding just 2-3 of these to your next build-up, not all 20 at once * #11 (micro-timing push) and #12 (false drop) are the two techniques that actually separate top producers from everyone else — most people never even try these * #14-20 are composer-level, not producer-level — this is the gap between "makes beats" and "writes music" ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "humanize": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🎹 HUMANIZING GUIDE — Velocity Per Element, Per Hit ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ Flat, identical velocity on every hit is what makes a programmed part sound programmed — applies to ANY instrument, not just drums: keys, plucks, bass, percussion Below is a concrete 8-hit reference table — an alternating strong/weak pattern per instrument. Use these as a starting point, then nudge individual hits by a few points so no two patterns in your track are ever byte-for-byte identical. ── 8-HIT VELOCITY REFERENCE TABLE ──────────────────── Instrument H1 H2 H3 H4 H5 H6 H7 H8 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── Closed Hi-Hat 95 62 78 58 90 60 76 55 Shaker 82 52 68 48 78 50 66 46 Kick 120 100 112 95 118 98 110 92 Snare 115 92 108 88 113 90 105 86 Clap 110 90 103 86 108 88 101 84 Perc/Rim 100 65 82 60 95 63 78 58 Open Hat 105 80 95 75 102 78 92 72 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── Reading the pattern: odd hits (1,3,5,7) sit on the strong 16th positions, even hits (2,4,6,8) sit on the weaker in-between positions — same alternating logic as the on-beat/off-beat idea, just laid out as exact numbers you can type straight into a piano roll. Micro-timing: ±5-15ms shift per hit — never perfectly on-grid, even with correct velocity values. ── ROLLS / FILLS — BUILD & DECAY EXAMPLE ───────────── A roll shapes a mini crescendo or decay across its hits, rather than sitting at one flat velocity throughout. Build-up roll (8 hits, getting louder toward the fill): Hit 1-8: 65, 70, 75, 80, 85, 90, 95, 100 Decay roll (used after a big hit, trailing off): Hit 1-6: 100, 88, 76, 65, 55, 45 Tip: Never use a perfectly even step size (e.g. always +5 every hit) — vary the increments too (+5, +4, +6, +5...) so it doesn't feel like a formula ── FLAMS / GHOST NOTES ─────────────────────────────── Flams: 2 layered hits 10-20ms apart, different velocities (e.g. 90 then 70) — never identical Ghost notes: Velocity 30-50, sit between the main hits — felt as texture, not consciously heard. Skipping these is the #1 giveaway of a programmed (vs. played) drum part ── KEYS / PLUCKS / MELODIC PARTS ───────────────────── Phrase peak: Velocity 90-100 — the emotional high point Phrase start: Velocity 70-85 — building into the peak Phrase tail: Velocity 50-65 — trailing off naturally Micro-timing: ±10-20ms — melodic parts can breathe more than rhythmic elements Tip: Shape velocity like a phrase, not per-note — think "building to a peak" not "random spread" ── BASS ─────────────────────────────────────────────── Downbeat hits: Velocity 95-105 — the anchor of the groove Syncopated hits: Velocity 70-85 — felt, not dominant Micro-timing: ±5-10ms only — bass needs to stay locked with the kick, don't drift too far Tip: Least timing variation of any element — bass/kick relationship is the groove's foundation ── ACCENTS (any element) ───────────────────────────── Structural hits: Velocity +15-25 above surrounding notes — deliberate, not random, tied to song structure Tip: Random variation reads as "noisy". Deliberate accents on structurally important beats read as "played by a person". Use both together. * Start with velocity variation first, add micro-timing second — velocity alone often gets 80% of the way there * MCS's MIDI Humanizer and Loop Kit Generator already apply this logic by default — same principle, tool-wide ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "illegal": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🧪 ILLEGAL PRODUCER TRICKS — Masterclass ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ "Illegal" is just a name — these are unusual/advanced production techniques, not literal rules. Some are meant to be subtle. Don't stack ten of these at once. ── PSYCHOACOUSTICS & PERCEIVED LOUDNESS ────────────── 1. Phantom impact — Thin out the last 100-300ms before the drop (remove sub/low-mid, not just volume). When full kick+bass returns, the drop feels harder without pushing the limiter harder. 2. Micro-silence before transients — A tiny 10-40ms gap right before a huge kick/impact. The ear briefly gets no info, so the next transient jumps out more. 3. Loudness without more peak — Add controlled harmonics via saturation/soft clipping instead of raising volume. Bass and synths can feel louder while peak barely moves. 4. Frequency starvation — Gradually remove frequency ranges before the drop: SUB gone → low-mid gone → top thinned → 💥 everything back. Feels full-range because the ear missed those frequencies. 5. Transient starvation — Same idea but with attack. Soften transients through the build (pads, reversed sounds, softened drums), then hit hard on the drop — transient contrast can do more than volume. ── STEREO / PHASE MADNESS ──────────────────────────── 6. Mono trap → stereo explosion — Narrow the last bar gradually (100%→70%→40%→near-mono), then FULL WIDTH on the drop. Keep kick/sub centered throughout. 7. Fake width, real center — Duplicate a texture/perc, treat L/R slightly differently (timing/pitch/filter), keep a strong central element. Width without falling apart. 8. Phase-transition FX — Automate a phaser/all-pass only during a transition, making the sound feel "unstable" right before the drop, then switch it off completely on impact. Chaos → sudden focus. 9. Haas fake-out — Brief small L/R timing offset on an FX/texture makes it feel huge-wide, then pull it back to center right before the drop. Avoid on sub/bass — always check mono. 10. Anti-width drop — Everyone expects a wide drop. Do a massive wide build → first drop hit in MONO → 1/4 bar later, STEREO EXPLOSION. Two impacts instead of one. ── RHYTHMIC DECEPTION ──────────────────────────────── 11. Fake downbeat — An impact/crash sounds like beat 1, but the real kick+sub land an 1/8 note later. Brief confusion, then the brain re-locks onto the groove. 12. Missing ONE — Drop starts with no kick on beat 1 (e.g. vocal → hat → KICK). The absence draws more attention than an extra kick would. 13. 3-over-4 infection — A perc accents every 3rd 16th while the track stays 4/4. Starts soft, gets louder every 2 bars until the groove feels like it's tilting — then drop it and the normal 4/4 feels rock-solid again. 14. Velocity polymeter — 16 hats, but a 5-step velocity cycle (e.g. 110-55-78-48-68 repeating). Since 5 and 16 don't align, every bar gets different accents while the MIDI notes stay identical. 15. Phantom tempo change — BPM stays fixed, but subdivide progressively faster (1/4→1/8→triplets→1/16→DROP). Brain perceives acceleration with no actual BPM automation — then you can drop into half-time afterward. 16. One-beat amnesia — For one beat right before the drop, remove almost everything that signals the grid (no kick, no snare, no clear hat — just a texture/vocal). Listener briefly loses the grid, then BOOM re-establishes beat 1. ── GHOST ENGINEERING ───────────────────────────────── 17. Invisible sidechain rhythm — Ghost triggers you don't hear duck bass/pads (kick → pump → [no kick but pump] → kick). A groove literally caused by inaudible drums. 18. Ghost transient — A very soft click/perc a few ms before a key snare/kick — not meant to be heard as a second sound, just primes the ear for the real hit. 19. Ghost reverb — Send a drum to reverb but make the dry drum itself inaudible. You hear a room reacting to something that doesn't exist — great before drops. 20. Ghost melody — A melody audible only through reverb/ delay before the drop, no dry signal. On the drop, the dry melody appears — brain thinks "why do I know this?" ── SOUND-DESIGN DECEPTION ──────────────────────────── 21. Future sound — Bounce your drop's main sound, reverse → stretch → filter → reverb, use THAT during the build. The drop announces itself before anyone realizes it. 22. Timbre morph — One sound unnoticeably becomes another (shaker→noise→riser→crash) via automated filter/pitch/ decay/distortion/reverb — four "instruments" become one continuous object. 23. Drum becomes synth — Take a tom/rim/kick-tail, extreme stretch, pitch it into key, add distortion/reverb — now it's a pad/drone/bass/texture, unified by shared source. 24. Synth becomes percussion — Reverse: take a synth stab, attack 0, decay extremely short, sustain 0, filter + transient processing — unique percussion nobody else from the same sample pack will have. ── DROP INSANITY ────────────────────────────────────── 25. Drop before the drop — Start the drop a fraction early vs. the expected phrase boundary — not enough to sound wrong, enough to trigger reflexive surprise. Confirm the real "1" right after. 26. Tiny drop → REAL DROP — Massive build, then a small dry kick + one vocal (almost disappointing), then ½ bar later: 💥 EVERYTHING. The "first drop" was really the last part of the build-up. 27. Drop eats itself — Drop starts full power, then after ~1 bar: FULL → LOW-PASS → MONO → SILENCE → immediately FULL DROP 2. Feels like the drop gets sucked in and explodes again. 28. Reverse expectation — Normally riser goes up into the drop. Instead: pitch/riser keeps climbing, then right before the climax, suddenly drops HARD DOWN into the drop. Listener expected more rise; you pull the floor out. 29. The impossible fill — Fill starts as normal 1/16s, then shifts to a triplet feel, then a few extremely fast hits ...STOP. Drop with something simple. Complexity→silence→ simplicity can hit harder than complexity→complexity. 30. THE FINAL BOSS — break multiple expectations at once. Build creates 3 expectations simultaneously: rhythm (expects beat 1 here), spectrum (expects sub back), stereo (expects width). On the expected drop: no kick, no sub, near-mono, one dry vocal/perc. "...?" A 1/4-1/2 bar later: KICK → SUB → FULL WIDTH → LEAD → TRANSIENTS. You didn't just make a loud impact — you denied three predictions at once, then resolved all three together. ── THE REAL TRICK BEHIND ALL 30 ────────────────────── Stop designing drops as BUILD → DROP. Think instead: Teach → Predict → Deprive → Confuse → Resolve The listener learns your pattern, starts predicting it, you remove one essential piece, brief doubt sets in, then you deliver the payoff. * The weirder the trick, the simpler the groove around it should be — a wild 3-over-4/phase/false-downbeat drop only feels "WTF?" when the listener knew exactly where the beat was before you broke it. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "aliensound": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ ⚡ ALIEN SOUND DESIGN WORKFLOW — Logic Pro ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ Four techniques for turning an ordinary MIDI melody into something strange, glitchy, and unmistakably "alien" — plus a layering trick to combine all four at once. ── 1. REVERSE CHUNKS ───────────────────────────────── 1. Bounce your MIDI track to audio (Ctrl+B, or right-click → Bounce in Place) 2. Double-click the audio → opens in the Audio Editor 3. Click Functions → Reverse 👉 Instant backwards, mysterious sound ── 2. PITCHSHIFTS ───────────────────────────────────── 1. Select your audio track → add Pitch Shifter (Audio FX → Pitch → Pitch Shifter) 2. Experiment with ±12 semitones (1 octave) or microshifts (±20 cents) 👉 For alien vibes: combine extreme shifts with delay/reverb ── 3. TIME-STRETCH ──────────────────────────────────── 1. Turn on Flex Mode (click the Flex icon above your track) 2. Choose Flex Time → Polyphonic (works best on melodies) 3. Stretch the audio: hold Option and drag a chunk longer/shorter 👉 Gives a glitchy or trippy effect ── 4. CHOP & RE-ARRANGE ─────────────────────────────── 1. Cut your audio into chunks (Command+T) 2. Shift them on the grid — or deliberately off-grid 3. Combine with reverse or pitch on individual chops 👉 Builds a completely new rhythm or alien melody from the same original chunk ── 🎯 PRO-TIP: LAYER ALL THREE ─────────────────────── Track 1 = original melody Track 2 = reversed chunks Track 3 = chopped and pitched version 👉 Together it sounds like a soundscape that's impossible to recreate — each layer processed differently from the same source material ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "vocalprod": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🎤 VOCAL PRODUCTION SECRETS ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ Techniques for making a vocal sit bigger, wider, and more confident in a mix — without leaning on heavy autotune. ── COMPING & TAKES ──────────────────────────────────── 1. Comp from 3+ takes — Record at least 3 full takes, then comp (combine) the best phrase from each. Even great singers rarely nail an entire take in one pass. 2. Punch-in on weak words — Don't re-record a whole line for one weak word — punch in just that word/syllable and blend the edit point inside a consonant, not a vowel. 3. Comp for energy, not just pitch — The most "in tune" take isn't always the best. Comp for the take with the most conviction/emotion, then fix pitch separately if needed. ── DOUBLING & LAYERING ──────────────────────────────── 4. Real doubles > pitched copies — Record the SAME line twice (not a duplicated/pitched copy) and pan hard L/R. Natural human timing variance creates real width that no plugin fully replicates. 5. Octave-up whisper layer — A near-silent, breathy octave-up double sitting far back in the mix adds "shimmer" and perceived size without adding audible loudness. 6. Stack harmonies low in the mix — Full harmony stacks at -15 to -20dB relative to lead vocal add richness the ear registers as "fuller" without consciously hearing harmony. ── SPACE & DEPTH ────────────────────────────────────── 7. Two reverbs, two jobs — Short room reverb (0.5-1s) for "glue" that sits right on the vocal, PLUS a separate longer plate/hall (2-4s) sent only from the loudest, most emotional phrases — depth without washing out clarity. 8. Pre-delay separates vocal from reverb — 20-40ms pre-delay keeps the dry vocal upfront and intelligible while the reverb tail still gives space — skip pre-delay and vocals can feel swallowed by their own reverb. 9. Automate reverb send by section — More reverb in verses (intimate), less in the hook (upfront, in-your-face) — static reverb sends make every section feel the same. ── DYNAMICS & PRESENCE ──────────────────────────────── 10. Two-stage compression — A fast, transparent compressor first (2:1, fast attack) to control peaks, then a second slower compressor (4:1, slower attack) for tone/character. One compressor doing both jobs usually sounds worse. 11. De-ess BEFORE compression — Compressing first can push sibilance louder, making the de-esser work harder than it needs to. De-ess early in the chain. 12. Automate word-by-word, not just phrase-by-phrase — Riding individual words up/down by ear (even -1 to +2dB) beats relying on a compressor alone for consistent presence. * The common thread: everything above is about controlled inconsistency — real doubles, riding words, varying reverb by section. Perfectly uniform vocals read as artificial. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "mixbus": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🧊 MIX BUS / GLUE TECHNIQUES ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ How individual elements stop sounding like separate layers and start sounding like one cohesive track. ── BUS COMPRESSION ──────────────────────────────────── 1. Low ratio, slow attack, auto release — 2:1 ratio, attack 10-30ms (lets transients through), release set to "auto" or matched to tempo. Aim for only 1-3dB of gain reduction on the loudest moments — glue is subtle, not obvious. 2. Group before you glue — Bus your drums together, your vocals together, your music elements together FIRST, each with light compression, before hitting a master bus compressor. Glue happens in layers, not just at the end. 3. Sidechain the whole mix bus to the kick — A very gentle (0.5-1dB) mix-bus duck triggered by the kick, barely audible, makes everything feel rhythmically connected to the low end without an obvious pumping effect. ── PARALLEL PROCESSING ──────────────────────────────── 4. Parallel compression on drums — Duplicate your drum bus, crush the duplicate HARD (10:1+, fast attack), blend it under the clean drums at 20-40%. Adds punch and perceived loudness without losing the original transients. 5. Parallel saturation on the full mix — A saturated duplicate of the whole mix blended in subtly (10-15%) adds harmonic glue and warmth that EQ alone can't replicate. ── TONAL COHESION ───────────────────────────────────── 6. Shared reverb space — Send multiple elements (vocal, lead synth, snare) to the SAME reverb bus instead of separate instances. Sharing one space makes them feel like they're performing in the same room. 7. Complementary EQ carving — If two elements compete in the same frequency range (e.g. vocal and lead synth at 2-4kHz), carve a small notch out of ONE of them at the other's peak frequency — they'll coexist instead of masking each other. 8. One saturation "flavor" across the mix — Using the same saturation plugin/character on multiple elements (drums, bass, master bus) ties them together tonally, even at very subtle amounts. ── REFERENCE & TRANSLATION ──────────────────────────── 9. Mono-check constantly — If the mix falls apart or loses energy in mono, elements aren't gluing — they're relying on stereo tricks to mask a lack of real cohesion. 10. A/B against a reference track — Match perceived loudness first (use a loudness meter, not just faders), then compare tonal balance. Never judge glue against a louder reference — louder always sounds "better" and misleads your ears. * Glue isn't one plugin — it's several small, mostly inaudible decisions (shared reverb, matching saturation, gentle bus compression) that together make a mix feel like ONE thing. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "samplechop": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🔪 SAMPLE CHOPPING WORKFLOW ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ Turning a sample into something that sounds like yours, not a loop with drums added on top. ── FINDING THE CHOP POINTS ──────────────────────────── 1. Chop on transients, not the grid — Zoom in and slice exactly where a note/syllable starts, not on the nearest bar line. Off-grid-but-on-transient chops sound cleaner than grid-perfect-but-off-transient ones. 2. Isolate the "money" moment — Find the single most interesting 1-4 seconds (a vocal ad-lib, a chord stab, a fill) and build the whole flip around just that piece rather than using the sample's full original phrase. 3. Chop smaller than you think — A sample chopped into 1-2 word/note pieces gives far more rearrangement freedom than chopping into full 4-bar phrases. ── REARRANGING ──────────────────────────────────────── 4. Reverse the "answer," keep the "question" forward — In a call-and-response phrase, try reversing just the response half — instantly sounds re-composed, not looped. 5. Repitch chops to a new scale — Pitch individual chops to fit a chord progression the original sample never had — turns a melodic sample into harmonic material you control. 6. Build a new rhythm from old syllables — Rearrange vocal chops purely for their percussive/rhythmic quality, ignoring the original lyrical meaning entirely. 7. Layer two different chops from the same sample — A low chop (pitched down, filtered) under a high chop (pitched up, bright) from the SAME source sample creates cohesion other producers flipping the same sample won't have. ── MAKING IT UNRECOGNIZABLE (WHEN YOU WANT THAT) ────── 8. Formant-shift + pitch separately — Most pitch shifters also shift formants by default. Shifting them independently (pitch up, formant down, or vice versa) disguises the original voice/instrument character completely. 9. Granular stretch on a single chop — Extreme time-stretch (300%+) on just one short chop turns it into a texture/pad — useful as an intro/breakdown element from the same sample. 10. Chain 2-3 subtle effects instead of 1 heavy one — A little EQ + a little saturation + a little pitch drift disguises a sample's origin better than one obvious, heavy effect. ── WORKFLOW SPEED ───────────────────────────────────── 11. Build a "chop bank" per session — Before arranging, chop everything you might want first and drag them to unused tracks/pads. Arranging from a ready bank is much faster than chopping mid-arrangement. 12. Name your chops as you go — "vox_hi_bright", "vox_low_ dark" beats "Audio 14" — you'll actually reuse chops you can find later instead of re-chopping from scratch. * The goal isn't just "does it sound different" — it's "does it sound like MY idea," built from someone else's raw material rather than their raw material with drums on top. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "transitions": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🎬 TRANSITION DESIGN ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ Making the moves BETWEEN sections as intentional as the sections themselves — verse→hook shouldn't just be a cut. ── THE FOUR TRANSITION TYPES ────────────────────────── 1. The riser — Builds tension going INTO a new section. White noise sweep, pitched riser, or a reversed cymbal — 8-16 bars leading into the target section, volume/filter automated to peak right at the downbeat. 2. The drop-out — Removes energy right before the new section (1 beat to 1 bar of near-silence or a single sustained element) so the new section's entrance feels like a release rather than a continuation. 3. The fill — A drum fill, vocal ad-lib, or instrumental run that occupies the LAST bar of the outgoing section, signaling "something is about to change" rhythmically. 4. The hybrid — Combine two: drop-out for 2 beats, THEN a short fill on beats 3-4 — more sophisticated than either alone, common in polished commercial productions. ── WHAT MAKES A TRANSITION FEEL INTENTIONAL ─────────── 5. Match the transition's energy to what follows — A big riser into a QUIET section feels mismatched — the transition should preview the destination's energy, not just build hype indiscriminately. 6. Automate more than one parameter — Volume + filter + reverb send moving together reads as "designed." Volume alone often reads as "just a fade." 7. Reuse a transition sound as a motif — If your riser/impact sound reappears at EVERY major transition (verse→hook, hook→verse), it becomes a recognizable signature that ties the whole track together. 8. Vary transition length by importance — Save your biggest, longest transition for the most important structural moment (intro→first hook). Smaller transitions between verse/hook repeats can be shorter — not everything needs an 8-bar buildup. ── PRACTICAL TECHNIQUES ─────────────────────────────── 9. Filter automation over 4-8 bars — Automate a low-pass filter opening from ~500Hz to fully open over the last 4-8 bars of a section — classic, reliable "opening up" feeling into the next part. 10. Pitch-bend the whole bus — A subtle pitch drop (a few cents to a semitone) on the last beat before a transition, automated back to normal after — adds a physical "lean into it" feeling. 11. Silence is a transition too — Don't default to always filling transitions with sound. A clean half-beat of true silence before a hook hits can be more impactful than any riser. 12. Automate reverb size, not just amount — A reverb whose ROOM SIZE grows through a build (not just wet/dry mix) creates a genuine sense of space opening up, distinct from a volume swell. * Test: mute everything except your transition element and listen to it alone. If it doesn't clearly signal "something is about to change" on its own, it's not doing its job yet. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "automation": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 📊 AUTOMATION STORYTELLING ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ Using automation to make a track feel like it's moving through a journey, not just repeating a loop with variations. ── BEYOND VOLUME ────────────────────────────────────── 1. Filter as a "focus" tool — Automating a low-pass filter open/closed doesn't just add energy — it directs attention. Close it on secondary elements during a vocal line to push focus toward the vocal without touching its volume. 2. Pan movement tells the ear where to look — A synth panning slowly left-to-right over 8 bars creates motion and interest even if nothing else about the sound changes. 3. Reverb/delay send as emotional distance — More send = further away, more "memory-like." Automating a vocal's reverb send UP right as it goes into a flashback-style lyric is a subtle but real emotional cue. 4. Stereo width as intimacy control — Narrow width = close, personal. Wide width = big, open. Automating width per section (narrow verse → wide hook) reinforces the emotional scale shift without touching EQ or volume. ── BUILDING A JOURNEY ───────────────────────────────── 5. Never repeat automation identically — If verse 2 uses the exact same automation curves as verse 1, it will feel static even if the melody differs. Nudge something — filter opens slightly more, a new element gets a swell. 6. One element evolves across the WHOLE track — Pick one element (a pad, a texture, a vocal ad-lib) and automate it slightly differently every time it appears — same part, evolving treatment — gives long-form cohesion. 7. Automate arrangement density, not just volume — Track how many elements are playing at once per section — automating WHEN elements enter/exit (not just their volume) is what actually creates a sense of progression. 8. Save your biggest automation move for the final chorus — A filter/width/reverb move you haven't used anywhere else in the track, saved for the last hook, makes the ending feel like a genuine climax rather than a repeat. ── PRACTICAL DETAILS ────────────────────────────────── 9. Curve shape matters as much as the values — A linear ramp feels mechanical. An exponential or S-curve automation shape (slow start, fast middle, slow end) feels more like a natural human gesture. 10. Automate in context, not solo — Automation that sounds great soloed can disappear in the full mix. Always draw/adjust automation while the whole track is playing. 11. Layer short and long automation together — A slow 16-bar filter build PLUS small per-bar volume nudges on top feels more alive than one long, smooth curve alone. 12. Leave some sections completely static — Not every bar needs movement. A deliberately static, unchanging section right before a big automated build makes the build itself hit much harder by contrast. * The test: play the track and close your eyes. If you can tell roughly where you are in the song just from the FEEL of the automation (not the melody), it's telling a story. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "genrepocket": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🥁 GENRE POCKET & GROOVE ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ What actually makes a beat "feel" like its genre — beyond just BPM and drum sample choice. ── TRAP / HIP-HOP ───────────────────────────────────── 1. Hi-hat rolls speed up gradually — A hat roll that accelerates (not a fixed rapid subdivision) feels far more "trap" than a static fast roll. 2. 808 glide, not just pitch — 808 bass notes that GLIDE between pitches (portamento) rather than jumping cleanly is a defining trap-pocket signature. 3. Snare sits slightly behind the beat — A few ms of deliberate lateness on the snare/clap (not the kick) creates the laid-back trap pocket — too on-grid feels stiff. 4. Kick avoids the snare's frequency AND its timing — Trap kicks often deliberately land in the gaps between snare hits rather than stacking directly under them. ── HOUSE ─────────────────────────────────────────────── 5. Kick on every beat, hats slightly swung — The 4-on-the- floor kick stays perfectly on-grid, but the off-beat hats get 5-15% swing — that contrast (rigid kick, loose hats) IS the house groove. 6. Open hat on the "and" — An open hi-hat on the off-beat "and" (between kicks) is one of house's most recognizable rhythmic signatures — try removing it to hear how much it's doing. 7. Bassline syncopation against a straight kick — The bass rhythm should mostly AVOID landing exactly on the kick — the interplay between straight kick and syncopated bass creates the "bounce." ── BOOM-BAP ──────────────────────────────────────────── 8. Swing on the 16th-note grid, not the 8th — Boom-bap swing is usually subtler and applied at the 16th-note level (55-58% swing), giving a "dusty," human MPC-style feel rather than an obviously shuffled rhythm. 9. Slightly detuned/dirty samples — A tiny bit of pitch drift or bit-crushing on drum samples (not clean, modern hits) is core to the boom-bap aesthetic — too clean reads as the wrong genre entirely. ── AFROBEATS / DANCEHALL-INFLUENCED ─────────────────── 10. Percussion polyrhythm over a simple kick — Keep the kick pattern minimal and let shakers/congas/log drums carry interlocking polyrhythmic patterns against it — busy percussion + simple kick, not the other way around. 11. Call-and-response in the drum pattern itself — Two percussion elements that "answer" each other rhythmically (one plays, pauses, the other fills the gap) creates the conversational groove feel central to the genre. ── UNIVERSAL POCKET PRINCIPLES ──────────────────────── 12. The kick and bass relationship defines the genre more than any single drum sound — study WHERE the bass sits relative to the kick (under it, around it, syncopated against it) more than what samples you're using. 13. Record a live "feel" pass and quantize only partially — Play a pattern in manually, then quantize to 50-70% strength instead of 100% — keeps genuine human timing variance that programmed grids default away from. * Groove isn't in the drum samples — it's in the relationship between elements: what's on-grid, what's not, and by exactly how much. Two producers with identical samples can make completely different-feeling beats from timing alone. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "edmfeelgood": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🌞 EDM / FEEL-GOOD PRODUCTION SECRETS ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ What separates a track that sounds "happy" on paper (major key, upbeat tempo) from one that actually FEELS euphoric. ── THE EUPHORIA FORMULA ─────────────────────────────── 1. Layer major 7ths and 9ths, not just triads — Plain major chords can sound generic/flat. Adding the 7th or 9th (even subtly, in a pad layer) gives that "shimmering, emotional" quality associated with big room / melodic EDM drops. 2. Wide, detuned supersaws — Multiple sawtooth oscillators slightly detuned from each other (5-15 cents apart) and spread across the stereo field is the core of that huge, euphoric EDM lead sound — a single clean oscillator rarely gets there alone. 3. Sidechain EVERYTHING to the kick, subtly — Not just bass — pads, leads, and vocals ducked 1-3dB on the kick creates the pumping, alive feeling core to EDM's energy, even when it's too subtle to consciously notice. 4. Vocal chops as a percussive/melodic hybrid — Short, pitched vocal chops used almost like a lead synth (not just as texture) is a defining feel-good/EDM technique — instantly human and euphoric in a way pure synths aren't. ── BUILD & DROP ARCHITECTURE ────────────────────────── 5. The "half-time" pre-drop — Cut the drum pattern to half speed for the final 2-4 bars before a drop — makes the full-speed return feel like a release of pent-up energy. 6. White noise riser + a SECOND, different riser — Layer a classic white noise sweep with a distinct pitched riser (different character, e.g. a rising pluck arpeggio) — two risers with different textures feel bigger than one louder riser. 7. The drop's FIRST hit matters most — Spend disproportionate time on the very first transient of the drop (kick + sub + impact layered and precisely aligned) — everything after rides on how strong that first hit feels. 8. Melody enters 1-2 bars into the drop, not immediately — Let the drum/bass groove establish itself alone first, then bring in the main melodic hook — gives the drop room to breathe instead of everything hitting at once. ── ARRANGEMENT FOR "FEEL-GOOD" ──────────────────────── 9. Major key doesn't guarantee happy — check the melody's INTERVALS. Melodies that resolve upward and land on the 3rd or 5th of the chord feel more uplifting than melodies that resolve downward or land on the root repeatedly. 10. Bright, open high end — Feel-good EDM tracks tend to have more energy above 8kHz (shimmer, air, cymbals, bright synth harmonics) than darker genres — don't be afraid to let the top end breathe. 11. A genuine breakdown, not just a quiet verse — A real breakdown strips almost everything away (vocal + one pad, nothing else) rather than just lowering the volume of the full arrangement — the contrast is what makes the next build feel earned. 12. End on a high note, literally — Whatever your outro does, consider ending the final melodic phrase on an upward resolution rather than trailing off downward — leaves the listener on an "up," not a fade. ── PRODUCTION POLISH ────────────────────────────────── 13. Bright reverb, not dark — Plate or bright hall reverbs (rather than dark, warm rooms) suit the euphoric aesthetic — reverb character itself carries an emotional tone. 14. Automate filter + reverb together on the main lead — Opening the filter AND increasing reverb size together through a build (not separately) creates a more unified sense of the track "opening up" into the drop. * The common thread: feel-good/EDM production is about CONTRAST — quiet before loud, narrow before wide, sparse before dense. The "good feeling" comes from the release, not just from major chords and a fast tempo. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "dawchords": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🎹 DAW CHORDS — How to Draw Chords in FL & Logic ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ This guide shows you EXACTLY which notes to draw in your piano roll — FL Studio or Logic Pro. Copy these note positions directly into your DAW. ── HOW TO READ THESE DIAGRAMS ──────────────────────── Each diagram shows a piano roll view: ■ = note ON (draw this note) · = note OFF (empty) Numbers = MIDI note position (C3, D3, E3 etc.) Duration guide: Whole note = 1 bar Half note = 1/2 bar Quarter note = 1/4 bar (1 step in FL) ── C MINOR (Cm) ────────────────────────────────────── Notes: C3 — Eb3 — G3 Piano roll view (1 bar): G3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ Eb3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ C3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ In FL Studio: → Open piano roll → draw C3, Eb3, G3 → Start all 3 at position 1:1 → Length: 1 bar each → Velocity: 80-90 for natural feel In Logic Pro: → Open piano roll → pencil tool → Click C3, Eb3, G3 at bar 1 → Drag to make 1 bar long each ── A MINOR (Am) ────────────────────────────────────── Notes: A2 — C3 — E3 Piano roll view (1 bar): E3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ C3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ A2 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ The most common minor chord in R&B and soul. Beyoncé tracks often use Am as the home chord. ── F MINOR (Fm) ────────────────────────────────────── Notes: F3 — Ab3 — C4 Piano roll view: C4 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ Ab3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ F3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ Dark, emotional — perfect for cinematic tracks. ── C MAJOR (C) ─────────────────────────────────────── Notes: C3 — E3 — G3 Piano roll view: G3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ E3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ C3 ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ Bright and uplifting. Gospel, pop, uplifting R&B. ── COMMON PROGRESSIONS IN DAW ─────────────────────── ★ BEYONCÉ / R&B PROGRESSION (Am — F — C — G) ───────────────────────────────────────────── Bar 1: A2+C3+E3 (Am) Bar 2: F3+A3+C4 (F) Bar 3: C3+E3+G3 (C) Bar 4: G2+B2+D3 (G) How to draw in FL Studio: → Open piano roll → Bar 1 pos 1:1: draw A2, C3, E3 — length 1 bar → Bar 2 pos 2:1: draw F3, A3, C4 — length 1 bar → Bar 3 pos 3:1: draw C3, E3, G3 — length 1 bar → Bar 4 pos 4:1: draw G2, B2, D3 — length 1 bar ★ EMOTIONAL / CINEMATIC (Cm — Ab — Eb — Bb) ───────────────────────────────────────────── Bar 1: C3+Eb3+G3 (Cm) Bar 2: Ab2+C3+Eb3 (Ab) Bar 3: Eb3+G3+Bb3 (Eb) Bar 4: Bb2+D3+F3 (Bb) ★ RIHANNA / POP FEEL (Fm — Db — Ab — Eb) ───────────────────────────────────────────── Bar 1: F3+Ab3+C4 (Fm) Bar 2: Db3+F3+Ab3 (Db) Bar 3: Ab2+C3+Eb3 (Ab) Bar 4: Eb3+G3+Bb3 (Eb) ── CHORD VOICINGS IN THE PIANO ROLL ───────────────── ROOT POSITION (strongest, most stable): Bottom note = root C minor: C3 at bottom → Eb3 → G3 at top 1ST INVERSION (softer, flowing): Bottom note = 3rd of the chord C minor inverted: Eb3 at bottom → G3 → C4 at top How to invert in FL Studio: → Select all notes of the chord → Hold SHIFT + scroll up/down to move octaves → Or manually drag the bottom note up an octave ── VELOCITY TIPS FOR NATURAL FEEL ─────────────────── In FL Studio — right click note → velocity: Strong beat (1 and 3): velocity 90-100 Weak beat (2 and 4): velocity 70-80 Ghost notes: velocity 30-50 In Logic Pro: → Select notes → bottom panel → velocity slider → Same rules apply ── ADDING MOVEMENT TO CHORDS ──────────────────────── Instead of playing all notes at once (block chord), play them one by one = BROKEN CHORD. This makes it feel alive like a real pianist. BLOCK CHORD (boring, static): All 3 notes start at the same time: G3 ████████████████ Eb3 ████████████████ C3 ████████████████ 1 2 3 4 BROKEN CHORD (moving, alive): Each note starts separately: G3 · · ████ · · · Eb3 · ████ · · ████ C3 ████ · · · · · 1 2 3 4 How to draw in FL Studio / Logic: ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Beat 1 (pos 1:1) → draw C3 alone │ │ Beat 2 (pos 1:2) → draw Eb3 alone │ │ Beat 3 (pos 1:3) → draw G3 alone │ │ Beat 4 (pos 1:4) → draw Eb3 alone │ │ Then repeat the same for bar 2... │ └─────────────────────────────────────┘ Each note = 1/4 length (one step in FL Studio) The chord is still C minor — you just play it differently. Same harmony, more movement. TIP: This works great on piano, pluck and Rhodes. This creates movement while keeping the same harmony. Perfect for piano and pluck sounds in Omnisphere. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ * These exact note positions work in FL Studio, Logic Pro, Ableton, GarageBand and any other DAW. MIDI notes are universal — same in every software. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", "compose": """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🎼 COMPOSITION TECHNIQUES — From Loop to Music ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ ── CALL & RESPONSE ─────────────────────────────────── What: Musical conversation — question and answer Like: A sentence spoken → a sentence replied Call (question): Rising melody, ends unresolved Response (answer): Falling melody, ends on root note Example in C minor: Call: C → Eb → G → Bb (goes up, leaves you hanging) Response: Ab → G → Eb → C (comes back down, resolved) How to use: → 2 bars of call, 2 bars of response = 4 bar phrase → Vary the response each time — same question, new answer → The response doesn't have to use the same notes ── COUNTERMELODY ───────────────────────────────────── What: A second melody that plays alongside the first Like: Two people singing different things that fit together Rules: → Counter moves OPPOSITE to the main melody If main goes up, counter goes down → They should land on chord tones at the same time → Counter should be softer than the main melody → Different rhythm than the main — creates interest Easy method: 1. Write your main melody 2. Find the chord tones at each bar 3. Write a slower-moving counter that hits those tones 4. Make it move in opposite direction ── MOTIF DEVELOPMENT ───────────────────────────────── A motif = a short musical idea (2-4 notes) Great music develops one motif in many ways Your motif: ta-ta, ta-ta-ta (like you described) Development techniques: → Repetition: Play it again exactly (establish it) → Sequence: Move it up or down a step each time → Inversion: Flip it upside down — go the other way → Augmentation: Make the notes longer (slower) → Diminution: Make the notes shorter (faster) → Fragmentation: Only use the first 2 notes of it → Development: Add a surprise note at the end Beyoncé example: The melodic hook in "Halo" is built on a 3-note motif repeated, sequenced and inverted throughout the song ── THE 4-BAR PHRASE ────────────────────────────────── Professional music is built in 4-bar phrases Each phrase has a shape: Bar 1: State your idea (call/motif) Bar 2: Develop it slightly Bar 3: Build tension — rise or intensify Bar 4: Resolve — land on a resting note Then the next 4-bar phrase begins — but changed ── TENSION & RELEASE ───────────────────────────────── ALL great music is about tension and release Without tension, music feels flat and boring Create tension: → Rise to the 7th of the scale (unstable note) → Use a sus4 chord (wants to resolve to major) → Increase rhythm density (more notes = more energy) → Dynamics — get louder approaching the peak Create release: → Land on the root note → Return to the major chord → Slow down the rhythm → Get softer after the peak ── AVOIDING THE LOOP FEELING ──────────────────────── The loop feeling happens when: → Same rhythm every bar → Same dynamics throughout → No variation in the melody shape → No 4-bar phrase structure Fix it: → Change something every 2 bars → Let the melody breathe — use rests → Vary the rhythm subtly each phrase → Build and release energy across 8-16 bars ── 8-BAR SONG STRUCTURE ───────────────────────────── Bars 1-2: Introduce your motif Bars 3-4: Develop it — move it up or change rhythm Bars 5-6: Build tension — rise to the high note Bars 7-8: Resolution — back to root, breath before next section ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ * Great composers repeat ideas — but always vary them The listener should recognize the motif AND be surprised by what you do with it each time ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""", } CONTENT["house"] = """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🏠 HOUSE MUSIC FUNDAMENTALS ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ House has its own rulebook — different from cinematic or trap. Get these 4 pillars right and everything else clicks into place. ── 1. GROOVE — THE FOUNDATION ──────────────────────── Four-on-the-floor: kick on EVERY beat (1, 2, 3, 4) — this is non-negotiable in house. Hi-hats on the off-beats (the "and" between the kicks) — this is what creates the forward motion/stuwing. Sidechain compression: everything EXCEPT the kick ducks down briefly every time the kick hits. This pumping effect is THE signature house sound — without it, a track sounds flat no matter how good the sounds are. → Ratio 4:1-8:1, fast attack, release matched to tempo ── 2. ARRANGEMENT — SONG STRUCTURE ─────────────────── House works in blocks of 8/16/32 bars, not free-form pop structure: INTRO (16-32 bars) Drums/percussion only — DJs need this to beatmatch in BUILD Add one layer at a time: bass → chords → lead Never dump everything in at once DROP / MAIN GROOVE Full energy, all layers together BREAKDOWN Pull the kick OUT — let pad/chords/vocal breathe alone This contrast is what makes the next drop hit harder OUTRO (16-32 bars) Back to drums only — DJs need this to mix out ── 3. SOUND SELECTION ──────────────────────────────── Classic house uses only 4-5 elements — never more: Kick · Bass · Pluck/Lead · Chord Stab · Pad Each element gets its OWN frequency space — nothing should overlap or fight for the same range. (See the Synth Sound Design Cheatsheet for exact ADSR/filter settings for each of these 5 sounds) ── 4. MIXING — MAKING IT "CLUB READY" ──────────────── → Keep everything below 100-150Hz MONO (kick + bass) → Sidechain everything to the kick (see Groove above) → Master loudness: -8 to -6 LUFS — louder than most other genres, this is normal for club playback → High-pass everything that isn't kick/bass, well above 100Hz — keeps the low end uncluttered ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ * Reference: your own House Pluck, House Bass, House Chord Stab, House Lead and House Pad presets in the Synth Sound Design Cheatsheet cover the sound-design side of all 5 core elements above. ── 5. DISCO DNA — WHY IT SOMETIMES DRIFTS "EMO" ────── House was born FROM disco — if a track loses that lineage, it drifts toward generic/melancholic ("emo") territory instead of feeling warm, danceable, and soulful. The fix is almost always harmonic, not arrangement. CHORD CHARACTER — the #1 culprit Minor triads alone read as sad/moody. Disco-house harmony is built on EXTENDED chords: maj7, m7, 9ths, add9, sus2. These carry warmth and soul without tipping into melancholy — this single swap is usually what separates "disco" from "emo" in a chord progression. → A plain Am triad feels moody. → Am9 or Am7 (add the 7th/9th) feels soulful instead. Stay mostly in MAJOR or DORIAN territory too — disco rarely lingers in natural minor for long; dorian's raised 6th is what gives it that lifted, hopeful feel even in a minor key. THE DISCO BASSLINE Not a static held note — a moving, syncopated, OCTAVE-JUMPING line that walks between chord tones. Root → octave → 5th → octave, with off-beat syncopation, is the classic shape. A static sub bass under a house beat is what makes a track feel flat/EDM instead of disco-rooted — the bass should groove on its own, not just sit there. STRINGS/PADS — the "orchestral lift" Disco's signature texture: lush, sustained string-like pads (real or sampled), often layered an octave apart, with a slow filter or volume swell. This is what gives disco-house its "uplifting" character even in a minor key — a thin synth pad alone won't carry that same warmth. THE FILTERED LOOP TECHNIQUE Classic disco-house move: take a short chord/instrument loop, chop it to a groove, and automate a lowpass filter sweeping open/closed in time with the arrangement. This filter-as-instrument approach (not just static EQ) is a core part of the genre's identity — silence in the low- pass is as much a "part" as the notes themselves. QUICK CHECKLIST if a track feels too emo: ☐ Swap bare minor triads for m7/m9 voicings ☐ Give the bass actual movement, not a held note ☐ Layer in a string/pad texture, not just one synth ☐ Automate a filter sweep somewhere in the arrangement ☐ Check you're not stuck in natural minor the whole way ── 6. MELODY — HOW IT ACTUALLY MOVES IN HOUSE ──────── House melody is a different animal from pop/vocal melody. Everything below is what separates a house lead that "sits in the mix" from one that fights it. LENGTH: SHORT AND LOOPED, NOT LONG AND SUNG Think 1-2 bar phrases that repeat, not a verse-length line that develops over 8 bars. The DJ/dancefloor connects through repetition and recognition, not through a story arc — a house lead is closer to a riff than a song melody. BUILT FROM THE CHORDS, NOT AGAINST THEM The most reliable way to write a house melody: take the notes of your chord progression and arpeggiate them (play them one at a time instead of together). This guarantees the melody is harmonically "inside" the track — no clashing, no extra music theory needed. Add a passing note or two once the arpeggio feels too predictable. RHYTHM: LOCKED TO THE GROOVE, NOT FLOATING OVER IT Place melody notes on the SAME off-beat positions as your hi-hats (the "and" of each beat), not squarely on the downbeats. This is what makes a lead feel like part of the groove instead of a vocal line dropped on top of it. Syncopation > straight quarter notes. SCALE CHOICE: STAY SIMPLE Minor/major pentatonic or a plain diatonic scale in your chosen key. Avoid chromatic runs or wide leaps — house melody works through hypnotic repetition, not complexity. A 3-5 note motif, repeated and lightly varied, outperforms a "clever" 8-note line almost every time. SPACE IS PART OF THE MELODY Leave gaps. A common shape: 2 bars of melody, 2 bars of rest (just the groove), repeat. The silence is what makes the return of the melody land — constant, unbroken melody reads as busy/cluttered against a four-on-the-floor groove. CALL AND RESPONSE (arrangement-level device) Split your motif into two halves and alternate them with a second element — e.g. lead plays phrase A, a vocal chop or stab answers with phrase B. This conversational structure is a classic house device for keeping a short, repeating motif interesting over a long arrangement without changing the notes. COMMON MELODIC "VOICES" IN HOUSE Arpeggio pluck — fast, short arpeggiated chord notes Stab — one held/short chord hit on select beats, more rhythmic device than melody Vocal chop — a sampled vocal snippet re-pitched to fit the chord tones, used melodically All three usually pull from the SAME chord tones — that's what keeps a house arrangement feeling unified even with several moving parts. PRODUCTION TOUCHES → Light humanization on timing/velocity (see the Humanize guide) — a perfectly quantized, identical- velocity melody reads as robotic/emo-adjacent by feeling emotionless rather than warm → A slow filter open on the lead's entrance mirrors the disco filtered-loop technique from section 5 → Sidechain the lead lightly to the kick too — keeps it from fighting the pump that defines the groove ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""" CONTENT["prolevel"] = """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🎧 PRO-LEVEL POLISH — GOING FROM DEMO TO PRO ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ You know the fundamentals now. This is what separates a solid track from one that sounds like Armin, David Guetta, or any top-tier house/dance producer — it's never one big trick, it's 4 layers of polish stacked. ── 1. LAYERING — MAKING SOUNDS FEEL "BIG" ──────────── Thin sounds are the #1 giveaway of a demo. Pros almost never use a single raw oscillator alone: → UNISON: stack 3-7 detuned copies of the same osc (detune 5-20 cents) — instant width and thickness → OCTAVE LAYERING: same sound doubled an octave up (thin/airy layer) AND down (weight/sub layer) → TEXTURE LAYER: add a quiet noise/vinyl/foley layer underneath leads — barely audible alone, but fills in the "gaps" between transients so nothing feels hollow → DOUBLE WITH A DIFFERENT WAVEFORM: e.g. a saw pluck layered with a quiet triangle/sine copy underneath — adds harmonic richness without changing the character ── 2. EMOTIONAL BUILD — THE "EUPHORIC" FEELING ─────── This is what Armin-style tracks nail: tension that actually pays off. → RISERS: white noise or pitch-rising synth over the last 4-8 bars before a drop — signals "something is about to happen" → FILTER SWEEPS: open a low-pass filter gradually across a build section — the "opening up" feeling → DROP THE KICK BEFORE THE DROP: silence or half-time for 1-2 bars right before impact — the contrast makes the drop hit twice as hard → LAYER ADDITIONS, NOT VOLUME: build tension by adding NEW elements each 4/8 bars, not just turning things up — gives the build actual musical movement → SIDECHAIN THE RISER slightly softer near the very end so the drop's kick cuts through cleanly ── 3. MIX DEPTH — THE BIG, WIDE PRO SOUND ──────────── → SEND BUSES: one shared reverb + one shared delay bus for the whole track — glues everything into the same "room" instead of each sound feeling separately mixed → PARALLEL COMPRESSION: blend a heavily compressed copy of your drum bus under the clean one — adds punch and density without losing dynamics → FREQUENCY CARVING: every element gets a tiny EQ cut where ANOTHER element already lives — this is what makes a pro mix sound like nothing is fighting → STEREO IMAGING: keep bass/kick mono and centered, spread mid/high elements (leads, pads, hats) wide — narrow low end + wide highs = the "pro width" trick → REFERENCE TRACK: A/B against a track you admire at matched loudness throughout the whole process, not just at the end (use the Audio Analysis + Reference Comparison tab for this) ── 4. MELODY / HOOKS — WHAT MAKES IT MEMORABLE ─────── → KEEP IT SIMPLE: the best hooks are 4-8 notes, repeated with small variations — not complex runs → CALL AND RESPONSE: a melodic phrase, then a "reply" phrase that answers it — creates a natural, singable shape → REPETITION WITH VARIATION: repeat the hook but change ONE thing each time (add a note, shift the rhythm, add harmony) — familiar but never boring → PLACE THE HOOK EARLY: the strongest melodic idea should appear in the first 30-45 seconds, not buried deep in the track → VOCAL CHOPS: chopping a vocal sample into short rhythmic stabs is a house/dance signature — try it as a percussive melodic layer, not just background ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ * None of this replaces good fundamentals — layer these on TOP of the House Fundamentals module. Pick ONE of these 4 areas per track and focus there; trying to nail all 4 at once usually backfires. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""" CONTENT["manualmaster"] = """══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ 🎚 MANUAL MASTERING IN LOGIC — REAL CONTROL ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ MCS's Apply Master tool is great for a fast, analyzed starting point — but real manual mastering gives you full control over every decision. This is how to master a single WAV file professionally in Logic, step by step. ── STEP 0 — PREPARE THE FILE ───────────────────────── → Import the WAV onto a fresh audio track — never master on top of your mix session, always a new project with just the stereo bounce → Check the bounce has headroom: peak should sit around -6 to -3dBFS BEFORE any mastering processing. If it's already hitting 0dB, ask for a version with more headroom — mastering a hot mix leaves no room to work → Label the track clearly (e.g. "MASTER — [artist] — [track] — v1") so nothing gets confused later ── WORKING FROM A SINGLE WAV — STAYING ULTRA CLEAN ─── No stems means no going back to fix one instrument — every move affects the WHOLE mix. That makes precision non-negotiable. This is how to keep the result clean: → NARROW, NOT WIDE: any EQ cut/boost should target the smallest range that fixes the issue (higher Q on Channel EQ). A wide EQ move on a full mix drags unrelated elements along with it — that's what causes "mud" or "smear" in a master → MID-SIDE EQ FOR SURGICAL CONTROL: switch Channel EQ to Mid-Side mode — cut mud (200-400Hz) more on the Sides than the Mid, since bass/kick (which needs to stay full) usually lives in the Mid. Keeps the low end punchy while cleaning the width → ONE MOVE AT A TIME: make a change, bypass it, listen, confirm it actually helped before adding the next one. Stacking untested moves is the #1 way a master ends up sounding processed instead of clean → IF THE MIX ITSELF IS THE PROBLEM: some issues (bad balance, muddy low-mids baked into the mix) genuinely can't be fixed at mastering without stems. Be honest rather than over-processing to compensate — heavy EQ/compression trying to "fix" a mix problem is exactly what makes a master sound like troep instead of clean. Note it and, if possible, ask for stems → LIMIT LAST, LIMIT GENTLY: an aggressive limiter on an already-imperfect mix amplifies every flaw instead of hiding it. If push comes to shove between "louder" and "clean," clean wins — MCS masters should sound controlled, not squashed ── STEP 1 — CORRECTIVE EQ (Channel EQ) ─────────────── Goal: fix problems, not add character yet. → High-pass at 20-30Hz — removes sub-sonic rumble that eats headroom without adding anything audible → Listen for one obvious problem frequency (boxiness around 300-500Hz, harshness around 2-4kHz) and cut it gently with a narrow-ish Q, -1 to -3dB → Resist boosting here — corrective EQ removes, it doesn't add. Save tonal shaping for Step 4 ── STEP 2 — GLUE COMPRESSION (Compressor) ──────────── Goal: make the mix feel like one cohesive thing. → Ratio: 1.5:1 to 2:1 — very gentle, this is NOT for loudness, it's for cohesion → Attack: 10-30ms — slow enough to let transients through, so drums keep their punch → Release: Auto (Logic's Compressor has a smart auto- release that adapts to the material — use it) → Aim for 1-2dB of gain reduction MAX on the loudest parts. If you see more, you're compressing too hard for this stage ── STEP 3 — REFERENCE TRACK COMPARISON ─────────────── → Import a reference track (a commercially released song in the same genre/vibe) onto a separate track → Use Logic's Gain plugin to level-match the reference to roughly the same perceived loudness as your master in progress — this is critical, a louder track always "sounds better" even if it isn't → A/B constantly between your master and the reference as you work through Steps 4-5 — trust your ears against a real released record, not just your memory ── STEP 4 — TONAL SHAPING (2nd EQ, after compression) ─ Goal: now shape the character/tone deliberately. → Low shelf, 100-150Hz, +0.5 to +1.5dB — subtle warmth, only if the reference track has more low-end weight than yours → High shelf, 8-10kHz, +0.5 to +1.5dB — subtle air/ brightness, same logic — only if needed vs reference → Small moves here. If you're reaching for +3dB or more at this stage, go back and fix it at the mix level instead — mastering EQ should be a polish, not a fix ── STEP 5 — LIMITING (Adaptive Limiter or Limiter) ─── Goal: bring up loudness safely, this is the final gate. → Set Output Ceiling to -0.3 to -0.1dB (never 0.0dB — leaves safety margin for lossy export/streaming codecs, which can overshoot slightly after encoding) → Raise the Gain/Input knob slowly, watching the Gain Reduction meter — aim for 3-6dB of reduction on the loudest peaks for a modern, competitive loudness → If you need more than 6-8dB of reduction to match your reference's loudness, the issue is earlier in the chain (mix balance or Step 2 compression), not something to force through the limiter alone → Target LUFS: streaming platforms normalize around -14 LUFS integrated, club/local files often run -9 to -6 LUFS. Check Logic's Loudness Meter (or a third-party LUFS meter) against your target ── STEP 6 — FINAL CHECKS BEFORE EXPORT ─────────────── → Check mono compatibility — sum to mono briefly (Logic's Direction Mixer or a Utility plugin) and make sure nothing disappears or phases out → Listen on at least 2 different systems — laptop speakers, then headphones/monitors, ideally also a phone speaker (MCS's System Emulation tool can help preview this digitally before a physical check) → Compare start-to-finish against the reference one more time, at matched loudness ── THE -9 TO -6 LUFS SWEET SPOT — RAP/VOCAL EQ ─────── This loudness range (louder than streaming-normalized -14 LUFS, common for rap/vocal-forward tracks meant to hit hard) needs different EQ decisions, because heavy limiting at this level exaggerates whatever is already in the signal — including problems. → DE-ESS BEFORE YOU LIMIT, NOT AFTER: sibilance ("s", "t", "sh" sounds) that's barely noticeable at -14 LUFS becomes genuinely harsh at -6 LUFS, because the limiter pushes those transient peaks up along with everything else. Use Logic's DeEsser 2 on the vocal bus (or the full mix if no stems) BEFORE the limiter, targeting 4-8kHz → PULL BACK 2-4kHz SLIGHTLY MORE THAN USUAL: this is where vocal presence AND harshness both live. At high loudness, a presence boost that sounded fine quiet can turn fatiguing — if the reference track is louder than yours and yours already has good presence, favor a small cut (-0.5 to -1.5dB) here instead of a boost → WATCH 1-3kHz FOR "SHOUTINESS": rap vocals pushed hard into a limiter often build up an aggressive, shouty quality in this range. A narrow, shallow cut (-1 to -2dB, moderate Q) here often cleans it up without losing intelligibility → KEEP LOW-END DISCIPLINED: at -6 to -9 LUFS the kick/ 808/bass sits right at the edge of the limiter's ceiling constantly — any low-end excess (below 80-100Hz) causes pumping and loudness inconsistency. High-pass more aggressively here than you would on a quieter master if the low end feels loose → TWO-STAGE LIMITING FOR CLEANER LOUD MASTERS: instead of asking one limiter for 6-8dB of reduction, use a gentle compressor (Step 2) PLUS the limiter, each doing less work — this keeps the vocal clear and present instead of squashed, even at high loudness → RECHECK DE-ESSING AFTER LIMITING: the limiter can still bring up sibilance that survived Step 1 de- essing. A quick pass with a second, gentle DeEsser after the limiter (or an EQ dynamic band at 6-8kHz) catches what got through ── STEP 7 — EXPORT ─────────────────────────────────── → Bounce as WAV, 24-bit, same sample rate as the original session (don't upsample/downsample unnecessarily) → Turn OFF any "normalize" option in the bounce window — you already set your levels intentionally, normalizing afterward can undo that → Keep a WAV master as the source file — only convert to MP3/AAC for specific delivery needs, never master from a lossy file ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════ * The order matters: correct → glue → reference-check → shape → limit → verify → export. Skipping straight to the limiter is the #1 reason masters sound flat or harsh — every step before it does real work. ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════""" if section == "progressions": content = self._gen_progressions_text() else: content = CONTENT.get(section, "Section not found.") # Each guide gets its own text color, matching its button color — # keeps the dark-bg readability while restoring per-guide distinction SECTION_COLORS = { "lefthand": "#e87070", "guitar": "#70a070", "sheet": "#70c8e8", "hihat": "#c8c830", "humanize": "#60c8a0", "illegal": "#e83060", "aliensound": "#40e8c0", "compose": "#e8a030", "dawchords": "#40c880", "progressions": "#c070e8", "house": "#40a0e8", "prolevel": "#e8323e", "manualmaster": "#40c880", "vocalprod": "#e870b0", "mixbus": "#70b0e8", "samplechop": "#e8905a", "transitions": "#a0e870", "automation": "#c8a0e8", "genrepocket": "#e8d060", "edmfeelgood": "#60d0e8", } txt.config(fg=SECTION_COLORS.get(section, "white")) txt.config(state="normal") txt.delete("1.0", tk.END) txt.insert("1.0", content) txt.config(state="disabled") def _gen_progressions_text(self): """Generate common chord progressions per genre, transposed into the currently selected key.""" NOTE_NAMES = ["C","C#","D","D#","E","F","F#","G","G#","A","A#","B"] key = getattr(self, 'pc_key', None) key = key.get() if key else "C" root = NOTE_NAMES.index(key) CHORD_INTERVALS = { "major": [0,4,7], "minor": [0,3,7], "dim": [0,3,6], "major7": [0,4,7,11], "minor7": [0,3,7,10], "dominant7": [0,4,7,10], } SUFFIX = {"major": "", "minor": "m", "dim": "dim", "major7": "maj7", "minor7": "m7", "dominant7": "7"} DEGREE_MAJOR = {"I":0, "ii":2, "iii":4, "IV":5, "V":7, "vi":9, "vii":11} DEGREE_MINOR = {"i":0, "ii":2, "III":3, "iv":5, "v":7, "VI":8, "VII":10} def chord_name(roman, quality, scale): degrees = DEGREE_MAJOR if scale == "major" else DEGREE_MINOR degree = degrees.get(roman.rstrip("7°"), 0) note = NOTE_NAMES[(root + degree) % 12] return f"{note}{SUFFIX.get(quality,'')}" def chord_notes(roman, quality, scale): degrees = DEGREE_MAJOR if scale == "major" else DEGREE_MINOR degree = degrees.get(roman.rstrip("7°"), 0) chord_root = (root + degree) % 12 intervals = CHORD_INTERVALS.get(quality, [0,4,7]) return " - ".join(NOTE_NAMES[(chord_root + i) % 12] for i in intervals) PROGRESSIONS = [ ("🎵 Pop", "major", [("I","major"),("V","major"),("vi","minor"),("IV","major")], "The most-used progression in modern pop — familiar, uplifting, easy to sing over."), ("🎤 R&B / Neo-Soul", "major", [("ii","minor7"),("V","dominant7"),("I","major7"),("vi","minor7")], "Jazzy ii-V-I movement with a 7th-chord vi — smooth, sophisticated, lots of room for melody."), ("🎬 Dark/Cinematic", "minor", [("i","minor"),("VI","major"),("III","major"),("VII","major")], "Classic minor-key cinematic loop — tension without resolving, keeps building."), ("🌙 Lo-fi", "major", [("ii","minor7"),("V","dominant7"),("I","major7"),("IV","major7")], "Jazzy and warm, built for looping — never fully resolves, stays relaxed."), ("🔥 Trap / Hip-Hop", "minor", [("I","major7"),("IV","major7"),("iii","minor7"),("V","dominant7")], "Warm, uplifting, churchy movement — great for empowerment/anthem tracks."), ("💔 Emotional Ballad", "minor", [("i","minor"),("iv","minor"),("VII","major"),("VI","major")], "Heavy, aching minor movement — sits well under a vulnerable vocal."), ] out = "══════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n" _generate_melody_notes(self): import random as rnd root = self.piano_key.get() mode = self.piano_mode.get() style = self.piano_style.get() n_bars = int(self.piano_bars.get()) SCALES = { "major": [0,2,4,5,7,9,11], "minor": [0,2,3,5,7,8,10], "dorian": [0,2,3,5,7,9,10], "phrygian": [0,1,3,5,7,8,10], "pentatonic":[0,2,4,7,9], } ROOT = {"C":60,"C#":61,"Db":61,"D":62,"Eb":63,"E":64, "F":65,"F#":66,"Gb":66,"G":67,"Ab":68,"A":69,"Bb":70,"B":71} NAMES= ["C","C#","D","Eb","E","F","F#","G","Ab","A","Bb","B"] PAT = { "melodic": [1,1,0.5,0.5,1,2], "trap": [0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5,0.25,0.25,1], "cinematic": [2,1,1,2,4], "ambient": [2,2,4,3,1], "emotional": [1,0.5,0.5,2,1,1], } root_m = ROOT.get(root, 60) scale = SCALES.get(mode, SCALES["minor"]) rhythm = PAT.get(style, PAT["melodic"]) total = n_bars * 4 notes = []; beat = 0; prev = 0; oct = 0 while beat < total: dur = rnd.choice(rhythm) if beat + dur > total: dur = total - beat if rnd.random() < 0.07: notes.append({"beat":beat,"dur":dur,"midi":None,"name":"R"}) else: if rnd.random() < 0.3: deg = rnd.choice(range(len(scale))) else: deg = max(0, min(len(scale)-1, prev + rnd.choice([-1,0,0,1,1]))) if rnd.random() < 0.15: oct = rnd.choice([-1,0,0,1]) midi = max(36, min(96, root_m + scale[deg] + oct*12)) name = NAMES[midi%12] + str(midi//12-1) notes.append({"beat":beat,"dur":dur,"midi":midi,"name":name}) prev = deg beat += dur return notes def _draw_piano_roll_on(self, notes, total_beats, bpm, canvas): canvas.update() W = canvas.winfo_width() or 250 H = int(canvas.cget("height")) canvas.delete("all") if not notes: return PAD_L,PAD_R,PAD_T,PAD_B = 24,4,4,18 pw = W-PAD_L-PAD_R; ph = H-PAD_T-PAD_B midi_vals = [n["midi"] for n in notes if n["midi"]] if not midi_vals: return mi = min(midi_vals)-1; ma = max(midi_vals)+1; mr = max(ma-mi,1) bw = pw/max(total_beats,1) NAMES=["C","C#","D","Eb","E","F","F#","G","Ab","A","Bb","B"] COLORS={0:"#c0392b",2:"#e67e22",4:"#f1c40f",5:"#2ecc71", 7:"#1abc9c",9:"#3498db",11:"#9b59b6"} # Grid beats = int(total_beats) for b in range(beats+1): x = PAD_L + b*bw c = "#222" if b%4!=0 else "#333" canvas.create_line(x,PAD_T,x,PAD_T+ph,fill=c) # Piano keys for midi in range(mi,ma+1): y = PAD_T+ph-int((midi-mi)/mr*ph) canvas.create_rectangle(0,y-3,PAD_L-2,y+3, fill="#1a1a1a" if midi%12 in[1,3,6,8,10] else "#2a2a2a", outline="#111") if midi%12==0: canvas.create_text(PAD_L-3,y,text=NAMES[midi%12], fill="#444",font=("Courier New",6),anchor="e") # Noten for n in notes: if not n["midi"]: continue x1 = PAD_L+n["beat"]*bw+1 x2 = PAD_L+(n["beat"]+n["dur"])*bw-1 y = PAD_T+ph-int((n["midi"]-mi)/mr*ph) col= COLORS.get(n["midi"]%12,"#4895ef") canvas.create_rectangle(x1,y-4,x2,y+4,fill=col,outline="#000") if x2-x1>12: canvas.create_text((x1+x2)/2,y,text=NAMES[n["midi"]%12], fill="white",font=("Courier New",6,"bold")) # BPM label canvas.create_text(W-2,H-4,text=f"{bpm}bpm", fill="#333",font=("Courier New",7),anchor="se") def _play_melody_idx(self, idx): if idx < len(self._melody_variants) and self._melody_variants[idx]: self._melody_notes = self._melody_variants[idx] if not self._melody_notes: messagebox.showwarning("Empty","Generate a melody first.") return self._melody_playing = False import time; time.sleep(0.05) self._play_melody() def _play_melody(self): if not self._melody_notes: return try: bpm = int(self.piano_bpm.get()) except ValueError: bpm = 80 self._melody_playing = True import threading, wave, struct, math, tempfile, subprocess as sp, os as os_ def midi_to_freq(m): return 440.0 * (2.0 ** ((m - 69) / 12.0)) def make_wav(freq, dur_s, sr=44100): """Maak een WAV bestand in temp directory.""" n_samples = int(sr * dur_s) tmp = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".wav", delete=False) with wave.open(tmp.name, "w") as wf: wf.setnchannels(1) wf.setsampwidth(2) wf.setframerate(sr) frames = [] for i in range(n_samples): t = i / sr # Envelope att = min(0.01 * sr, n_samples * 0.1) rel = min(0.1 * sr, n_samples * 0.3) if i < att: env = i / att elif i > n_samples - rel: env = (n_samples - i) / rel else: env = 1.0 val = (0.4 * math.sin(2*math.pi*freq*t) + 0.15 * math.sin(2*math.pi*freq*2*t) + 0.05 * math.sin(2*math.pi*freq*3*t)) frames.append(struct.pack(" 12 else "") out += f" {i+1}: {preview}\n" out += "\n── HOE TE GEBRUIKEN ───────────────────────────\n" out += " · Klik ▶ per variatie om te horen\n" out += " · Typ eigen noten bovenaan: C D E G\n" out += Knoppen br = tk.Frame(p, bg=BG); br.grid(row=8, column=0, sticky="w", pady=(6,0)) self._btn(br, " 🤖 Genereer met AI ", GREEN, "#090909", self._run_ai).pack(side="left", padx=(0,8), ipady=2) self._btn(br, "📋 Copy", BG4, BTN_FG, lambda: self._copy_txt(self.ai_txt)).pack(side="left", padx=(0,8)) self._btn(br, "⭐ Favorite", BG4, GOLD_LT, lambda: self._fav_txt(self.ai_txt)).pack(side="left", padx=(0,8)) self._btn(br, "🗑 Clear", BG4, BTN_FG, lambda: self._write(self.ai_txt, "")).pack(side="left") self.ai_status = tk.Label(p, text="", font=F_LABEL, fg=GREEN, bg=BG) self.ai_status.grid(row=9, column=0, sticky="w", pady=(4,4)) self.ai_txt = self._txt_out(p, 10, GREEN) p.rowconfigure(10, weight=1) self._key_visible = False def _save_api_key(self): key = self.ai_key_entry.get().strip() if not key: messagebox.showwarning("Empty","Voer eerst een API key in.") return try: data = {} if os.path.exists(DATA_FILE): with open(DATA_FILE,"r",encoding="utf-8") as f: data = json.load(f) data["api_key"] = key with open(DATA_FILE,"w",encoding="utf-8") as f: json.dump(data, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) self.ai_key_entry.config(fg=GREEN) messagebox.showinfo("✅","API key opgeslagen!") except Exception as e: messagebox.showerror("Error", str(e)) def _load_api_key(self): try: if os.path.exists(DATA_FILE): with open(DATA_FILE,"r",encoding="utf-8") as f: return json.load(f).get("api_key","") except Exception: pass return "" def _toggle_key(self): self._key_visible = not self._key_visible self.ai_key_entry.config(show="" if self._key_visible else "•") def _run_ai(self): key = self.ai_key_entry.get().strip() if not key or not key.startswith("sk-"): messagebox.showwarning("Geen API key", "Voer een geldige Anthropic API key in.\n\nKrijg er een op: console.anthropic.com") return task = self.ai_task.get() user_in = self.ai_input.get("1.0", tk.END).strip() lang = self.lang.get() # Bouw systeem prompt per taak if task == "titles": system = ("You are a professional music title generator for sync composers. " "Generate 10 unique, evocative track titles. " "Return only the titles, one per line, no numbering.") prompt = f"Generate 10 track titles for: {user_in}. Language: {'Dutch' if lang=='nl' else 'English'}" elif task == "bars": system = ("You are a professional rap lyricist and ghostwriter. " "Write 8 bars of rap lyrics with internal rhymes and flow. " "Return only the bars, no explanation.") prompt = f"Write 8 rap bars about: {user_in}. Language: {'Dutch' if lang=='nl' else 'English'}" elif task == "sync": system = ("You are an expert sync music supervisor and composer. " "Create a detailed professional sync briefing including: " "BPM range, key, chord progression, arrangement guide, " "instrument suggestions, scene types, and placement opportunities.") prompt = f"Create a sync music briefing for: {user_in}" elif task == "lyrics": system = ("You are a professional songwriter. " "Write lyrics including a verse, pre-chorus, and chorus. " "Focus on imagery and emotion.") prompt = f"Write song lyrics about: {user_in}. Language: {'Dutch' if lang=='nl' else 'English'}" else: system = ("You are a professional music industry assistant helping composers, " "producers and songwriters. Give expert, practical advice.") prompt = user_in self.ai_status.config(text="⏳ AI genereert... even geduld") self.update() import threading def ai_thread(): try: import urllib.request, json as json_lib payload = json_lib.dumps({ "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5", "max_tokens": 1024, "system": system, "messages": [{"role":"user","content":prompt}] }).encode("utf-8") req = urllib.request.Request( "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages", data=payload, headers={ "Content-Type": "application/json", "x-api-key": key, "anthropic-version":"2023-06-01" }, method="POST" ) with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as resp: result = json_lib.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8")) ai_out = result["content"][0]["text"] task_labels = {"titles":"Track Titels","bars":"Rap Bars", "sync":"Sync Briefing","lyrics":"Lyrics","custom":"AI Advies"} full_out = f"── AI GEGENEREERD: {task_labels.get(task,'').upper()} ──────────────\n" full_out += f" Prompt: {user_in[:80]}...\n" full_out += f"{'─'*50}\n\n" full_out += ai_out self._write(self.ai_txt, full_out) self.ai_status.config(text="✅ AI klaar!") self._save_hist("ai", task, user_in, [ai_out]) except Exception as e: err = str(e) if "401" in err: self.ai_status.config(text="❌ API key ongeldig — check console.anthropic.com") elif "429" in err: self.ai_status.config(text="❌ Rate limit — even wachten") else: self.ai_status.config(text=f"❌ {err[:60]}") self._write(self.ai_txt, f"Fout: {err}") threading.Thread(target=ai_thread, daemon=True).start() # ── SYNC KANSEN TRACKER ─────────────────────────────── numpy as np import subprocess, sys y, sr = librosa.load(self.audio_file, sr=None, mono=True, duration=90) duration = librosa.get_duration(y=y, sr=sr) # ── Analysis ────────────────────────────────── rms = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(y**2))) peak = float(np.max(np.abs(y))) peak_db = 20*np.log10(peak) if peak > 0 else -60 crest_db = 20*np.log10(peak/rms) if rms > 0 else 0 lufs_approx = 20*np.log10(rms) + 3.0 if rms > 0 else -60 S = np.abs(librosa.stft(y, n_fft=4096)) freqs = librosa.fft_frequencies(sr=sr, n_fft=4096) avg = np.mean(S, axis=1) total = np.sum(avg) + 1e-10 def bp(lo, hi): m = (freqs >= lo) & (freqs < hi) return float(np.sum(avg[m]) / total * 100) sub_e = bp(20, 80) low_e = bp(80, 250) lomid_e = bp(250, 1000) himid_e = bp(1000, 5000) high_e = bp(5000, 12000) air_e = bp(12000, 20000)
